attagenus-unicolor.summary: Black carpet beetles are small, dark, oval beetles whose young have a very different appearance and appetite. The narrow, brown, hairy larvae carry a long tuft at the rear and feed on wool, fur, feathers and other animal materials. Adults visit flowers for pollen and nectar and may enter buildings to lay eggs. Indoors, larvae can remain hidden in lint, stored textiles or insect collections; shed skins and irregular damage are often easier to find than the beetles themselves.

myzus-cerasi.summary: Black cherry aphids gather on tender cherry growth, where their glossy dark bodies stand out against the leaves. Feeding can curl sweet-cherry leaves tightly around the colony and distort young shoots. The aphids also leave sticky honeydew that can support dark sooty mold. Eggs spend the winter on cherry twigs, while later generations commonly move to plants in the mustard family for summer. Lady beetles, lacewings and other predators help limit their numbers in orchards.

sources.label: UC IPM — Cherry Pest Management Guidelines

aphis-aurantii.summary: Black citrus aphid is a small, dark sap-feeding insect found on soft new growth of citrus and many other plants. Coffee, cacao and ornamental shrubs are among its hosts. Colonies can curl or distort young leaves and deposit sticky honeydew, on which sooty mold grows. Despite its name, it is not restricted to citrus. Predators and tiny parasitic wasps often keep colonies in check, and the importance of this aphid varies with the crop and region.

hyoscyamus-niger.summary: Black henbane is a sticky, unpleasant-smelling member of the nightshade family that grows as an annual or biennial. It occurs along roadsides, fences and disturbed pastures, sometimes forming dense patches. Originally brought to North America for ornamental and medicinal use, it now grows outside cultivation in many areas. Its historical use should not suggest a safe household remedy: every part contains toxic alkaloids. A plant may spend its first season as a low rosette before producing an upright flowering stem.

sources.label: University of Nevada, Reno — Managing Black Henbane
Montana State — Black Henbane Identification, Biology and Integrated Management

solenopsis-richteri.summary: Black imported fire ants live in colonies with conspicuous soil mounds and workers of several sizes. Workers are mostly brownish black, sometimes with a reddish patch on the abdomen, and can deliver a painful sting. Introduced populations are established in parts of the southeastern United States. This species is closely related to the red imported fire ant and can hybridize with it, so color alone is not a reliable way to separate them. Specialist examination may be needed for a firm identification.

sources.label: University of Georgia — Managing Imported Fire Ants in Urban Areas

medicago-lupulina.summary: Black medick is a low, spreading member of the pea family often seen in lawns, field edges and disturbed ground. Its leaves have three small leaflets, giving it a clover-like appearance, but the central leaflet has a short stalk of its own. Rounded clusters of tiny yellow flowers develop into dark seedpods, which explain the common name. It often grows where turf is thin or soil is poor, and its taproot supports a mat of stems close to the ground.

mimosa-pigra.summary: Black mimosa is a prickly, woody shrub with finely divided leaves that fold when touched. Rounded pink to mauve flower heads are followed by clusters of bristly brown pods. It favors wet ground, including floodplains, stream edges and abandoned fields. Native to tropical America, it has become a major wetland invader in northern Australia, where dense stands replace open vegetation and obstruct access. Its sensitive foliage resembles that of smaller sensitive plants, but mature black mimosa forms a substantial shrub.

sources.label: USDA NRCS — Common Weeds in Puerto Rico and U.S. Virgin Islands

brassica-nigra.summary: Black mustard is an upright annual with bright yellow flowers and a loose rosette of lower leaves. The lower leaves are lobed, while leaves higher on the stem become narrow and undivided. Its short, slender seedpods stand close against the flowering stem, a useful distinction from several other yellow-flowered mustards. Mature plants can rise well above surrounding low vegetation. The plant is widely known under the name Brassica nigra, although modern taxonomic treatments sometimes place it in another genus.

sources.label: Flora of New Zealand — Brassica nigra

solanum-nigrum.summary: Black nightshade is a branching herb with small white flowers and clusters of berries that change from green to black or purplish black. It grows in sunny, disturbed places such as fields, gardens and roadsides. Birds can spread its seeds after eating the fruit. Identification deserves care: several closely related nightshades look alike, and New England records have often used this name too broadly. The leaves and unripe fruit contain toxic compounds, so appearance alone is no basis for treating it as food.

sources.label: Native Plant Trust — European Black Nightshade

jacaranda-mimosifolia.summary: Black poui, better known in many places as jacaranda, is a South American tree grown for its blue-purple flowers and fine, fern-like foliage. Its spreading branches create light shade, and the flowers can form a colorful carpet beneath the canopy. Rounded, woody seed capsules persist after flowering. It does best in warm conditions with sunshine and well-drained soil; frost limits where it can thrive. Its presence as a planted ornamental should be distinguished from evidence that it has escaped cultivation.

rattus-rattus.summary: Black rats are slender, agile rodents also called roof rats or ship rats. Their long tails help them balance as they climb trees, fences and buildings. They often nest above ground in dense vegetation, attics or wall spaces and forage mainly at night. Fruit and nuts are important foods, but their diet also includes small animals and eggs. Human transport has carried them far beyond their original range, and around buildings they can contaminate food and damage materials by gnawing.

parasaissetia-nigra.summary: This black scale, also called nigra scale, is a sap-feeding insect found on many tropical and subtropical plants. Adult females look like dark brown or glossy black bumps; they are broader on leaves and often narrower on twigs. Citrus, coffee, mango, avocado, hibiscus and figs are among its hosts. The young crawlers move to new feeding sites, while older stages are usually still. Feeding produces honeydew, and natural enemies can provide substantial control of colonies.

saissetia-oleae.summary: Black scale is a soft scale insect whose mature females resemble dark raised bumps on woody stems. A ridge shaped like the letter H is a particularly useful clue. Young stages settle on leaves and twigs, feeding on plant sap and releasing sticky honeydew. Sooty mold grows on that coating, and heavy colonies can weaken trees. Olive and citrus are familiar hosts, along with many ornamentals. Dense, sheltered foliage can favor the insect, while parasitoid wasps help restrain it.

sources.label: UC IPM — Black Scale in Olive

ctenosaura-similis.summary: Black spiny-tailed iguanas are large lizards with a long tail ringed by sharp scales. Adults are commonly gray or tan with dark bands, while young animals may retain green coloring. They bask in open places and shelter among rocks, walls or burrows. Young iguanas eat many insects; adults take more plant material but still consume animal prey. Native to Mexico and Central America, the species has established populations in Florida, where local wildlife impacts have been documented.

sources.label: UF/IFAS — Black Spiny-tailed Iguanas on Gasparilla Island

tubastraea-micranthus.summary: Black sun coral builds branching, tree-like colonies with dark green to black living tissue over a hard pale skeleton. Unlike many familiar reef corals, it lacks the symbiotic algae that supply energy from sunlight. Its polyps capture food carried by the water, and its strong skeleton suits places exposed to currents. Native to the Indo-Pacific, it has also been recorded growing on offshore platforms in the northern Gulf of Mexico. It is a stony coral, despite the name suggesting precious black corals.

sources.label: Schuhmacher — Reef-building properties of Tubastraea micranthus
Sammarco et al. — A new coral species introduced into the Atlantic

vincetoxicum-nigrum.summary: Black swallow-wort is a perennial climbing plant that winds around neighboring vegetation or trails across the ground. Its opposite, oval leaves are glossy green, and its small dark-purple flowers have five triangular lobes. In summer, slender pods develop and later release seeds with silky hairs. The plant comes from southwestern Europe and has established dense patches in parts of North America. Its twining stems and nearly black flowers help distinguish it from the more familiar upright milkweeds.

ischnaspis-longirostris.summary: Black thread scale is an armored scale insect with an unusually long, narrow protective cover. Adult females have yellow bodies hidden beneath shiny dark-brown to black covers that look like tiny dashes on a leaf or stem. It feeds on many tropical and subtropical plants, with palms among its common hosts. The yellow young crawlers disperse before settling to feed. Female reproduction does not require mating, and males have not been observed in the accounts used here.

sources.label: Naturalis — Diaspididae of the World: Ischnaspis longirostris

xylosandrus-compactus.summary: Black twig borer is a tiny beetle that tunnels into small branches of many trees and shrubs. Females make pin-sized entrances, often on the underside of a twig, and establish a chamber where their young develop. Fungi growing inside provide food for the beetles. Leaves beyond an attack may wilt and turn brown, making a dead twig the first obvious sign. Unlike many related ambrosia beetles, it can attack healthy plants as well as stressed ones.

otiorhynchus-sulcatus.summary: Black vine weevil is a dark, broad-snouted beetle that feeds at night and hides by day. Adults leave rounded notches around leaf edges, but the more serious damage usually happens below ground. Its pale, legless grubs eat roots and can cause container plants to wilt or die. Many ornamental plants and some fruits are hosts. Adults cannot fly, yet they climb well, and movement of infested plants can make this a persistent nursery and garden problem.

sources.label: University of Minnesota — Black Vine Weevil

acacia-mearnsii.summary: Black wattle is an Australian shrub or tree with finely divided leaves and rounded clusters of pale-yellow or cream flowers. The foliage gives the canopy a soft, feathery appearance, while its seedpods are narrow and often pinched between the seeds. In its native southeastern Australian range it grows in forest, woodland and coastal scrub, including creek banks and hillsides. It has been widely cultivated for tannin and timber products, so a planted tree does not by itself establish a local invasion.

sources.label: Royal Botanic Gardens Sydney — Acacia mearnsii

iris-domestica.summary: Blackberry lily is a perennial in the iris family, despite its lily-like common name. Fans of upright, sword-shaped leaves rise from underground stems, and wiry flowering stems carry orange blooms marked with red spots. Later, the seed capsules split open to show shiny black seeds clustered like a blackberry. Native to eastern and southeastern Asia, it is widely grown as an ornamental. The showy black clusters are seeds rather than edible berries, an easy distinction to miss.

thunbergia-alata.summary: Blackeyed susan vine is a twining plant with soft, triangular to heart-shaped leaves and flowers that usually have a dark central eye. Wild forms commonly flower in yellow or orange, while garden selections offer additional colors. Native to tropical and southern Africa and Madagascar, it grows in varied habitats from woodland edges to disturbed vegetation. In gardens its stems climb supports or trail from baskets. It is distinct from the upright North American Rudbeckia flowers that share the black-eyed Susan name.

acacia-melanoxylon.summary: Blackwood is an Australian tree with dark, deeply furrowed bark and a leafy crown that can reach forest-tree proportions. Its mature foliage consists of flattened leaf stalks, called phyllodes, with several strong lengthwise veins. Pale cream to yellow flower balls are followed by twisting brown pods; each dark seed is partly surrounded by a bright orange or reddish thread. In its native range it grows in moist forests, including wet eucalyptus forest and cooler rainforest.

sources.label: Plants of the World Online: Acacia melanoxylon

silene-latifolia.summary: The plant catalogued here as bladder campion is Silene latifolia, usually called white campion. This short-lived perennial has soft, hairy leaves in opposite pairs and white flowers with five deeply notched petals. Behind each flower is a swollen, veined green cup. Male and female flowers grow on separate plants. Native to Europe and introduced in North America, it grows in fields, meadows and disturbed ground. It can hybridize with red campion, producing plants with pink flowers.

silybum-marianum.summary: Blessed milkthistle is a large annual or biennial thistle whose glossy green leaves are boldly marbled with white. Sharp spines line the leaves and the broad bracts surrounding its pink-purple flower heads. Young plants begin as ground-level rosettes before sending up tall flowering stems. Originally from southern Europe, it has been cultivated as an herb and can escape into disturbed ground and pasture. Its conspicuous foliage helps separate it from many other thistles even before it flowers.

papaver-dubium.summary: Blindeyes, also called long-headed or field poppy, is a slender annual with hairy stems, divided leaves and delicate orange-red flowers. Its four petals may have little or no dark marking at their bases. The fruit is especially useful for recognition: a smooth, elongated capsule rather than the short, rounded capsule of some other poppies. Fine hairs lie flat against the upper flower stalk. A taproot anchors the plant, while its dry capsules release many small seeds.

sources.label: Flora of New Zealand: Papaver dubium

calliandra-haematocephala.summary: Blood red tassel flower is a tropical shrub or small tree grown for round, bright red flower clusters that resemble powder puffs. The showy threads are the flowers' long stamens. Its leaves are twice divided into small leaflets, giving the spreading crown a fine texture. Firm brown pods follow the flowers. Kew places its native range in Bolivia, while cultivated plants are familiar in warm gardens, where moist, well-drained soil and sun or partial shade suit its growth.

sources.label: Plants of the World Online: Calliandra haematocephala

asclepias-curassavica.summary: Bloodflower is a tropical milkweed with narrow, opposite leaves and clusters of red-orange flowers topped by yellow or orange crowns. Its upright stems release milky sap when damaged, and slender pods eventually open to release silky-haired seeds. It stays leafy in warm conditions but is often grown as an annual where winters are cold. Monarch caterpillars feed on it, yet persistent winter growth in warm regions can encourage parasite buildup, making locally native milkweeds a better garden choice there.

geranium-sanguineum.summary: Bloody geranium is a low, spreading perennial often grown in gardens for its magenta-pink flowers. Each flower has five broad petals marked with darker veins, while the leaves are deeply divided into narrow, fingerlike lobes. Underground stems allow a clump to widen over time. Native to Europe and western Asia, it favors well-drained ground in sun or partial shade. Garden escapes have been documented in parts of North America, including disturbed sites and meadows in New England.

hemimysis-anomala.summary: Bloody red shrimp is a tiny freshwater crustacean with prominent black eyes and a partly transparent body speckled red or orange. Its color changes with light and temperature, so some individuals look almost colorless. Swarms shelter around rocks, docks and other shaded structures, emerging to feed on small aquatic organisms. Native to the Ponto-Caspian region, it has spread to the Great Lakes. Its flat-ended tail, with a long spine at each corner, is more useful for identification than redness alone.

chrysomya-rufifacies.summary: This blow fly is often called the hairy maggot blow fly because its older larvae carry fleshy, spiny projections that give them a bristly appearance. Adults are metallic green with a bluish sheen and resemble several other blow flies. The larvae develop in animal remains, where older stages may also prey on other maggots. The species is important in forensic research and livestock health; in some regions it can infest existing animal wounds as well as carrion.

sources.label: Hairy maggot blow fly: Chrysomya rufifacies

acyrthosiphon-kondoi.summary: Blue alfalfa aphid is a soft-bodied, blue-green insect that feeds on alfalfa and other legumes. Long legs, antennae and paired rear tubes give it a slender appearance. Colonies often gather on young shoots and stems, especially in cool weather. Feeding can stunt plants, while sticky honeydew supports dark sooty mold. It closely resembles the pea aphid and may occur alongside it, but its antennae darken gradually toward the tips instead of carrying distinct dark bands at the joints.

sherardia-arvensis.summary: Blue fieldmadder is a small annual that can spread into a low, rough-textured mat. Narrow leaves and leaflike structures form rings around its square stems, making it resemble a miniature bedstraw. The tiny flowers set it apart: they are pinkish mauve, with a short tube opening into four spreading lobes, clustered near stem tips. Native across parts of Europe, North Africa and Asia, it also grows beyond that range in fields, grassland and other open, disturbed places.

sources.label: Flora of New Zealand: Sherardia arvensis

selitrichodes-globulus.summary: Blue gum galling wasp is a small insect whose larvae develop inside swollen growths on blue gum eucalyptus. The damaged shoots can look distorted and discolored, making the galls easier to notice than the adult wasps. The species was described scientifically in 2009 after infestations were found in Los Angeles County, California. Published accounts associate it with the blue gum complex; unusual eucalyptus galls on their own do not prove that this particular wasp is present.

sources.label: A new species of invasive gall wasp on blue gum in California

panicum-antidotale.summary: Blue panicum is a tall, coarse perennial grass that grows in dense clumps and spreads by short underground stems. Its sturdy stems have conspicuous joints, while the long leaves show a strong middle vein and often wavy margins. Loose, branching seed heads become drooping as they mature. Native to Asia and planted as a forage grass elsewhere, it can escape into open or disturbed ground. Texas records describe it in fields and other open sites, especially on clay loam soils.

crotalaria-verrucosa.summary: Blue rattlesnake is a bushy tropical legume, also known as blue rattlepod. Unlike many relatives with divided leaves, it has broad, simple leaves on angular, branching stems. The pea-shaped flowers are pale blue, lavender or whitish, with a darker keel, and are followed by short, inflated, softly hairy pods. Kew places its native range from tropical and subtropical Asia to northern Australia. Elsewhere in the tropics it occurs in open places, including pastures and sandy roadsides.

sources.label: Plants of the World Online: Crotalaria verrucosa
Digital Flora of Eastern Ghats: Crotalaria verrucosa

ophiostoma-tenellum.summary: The fungus catalogued as Ophiostoma tenellum is now called Jamesreidia tenella. It is a microscopic wood-associated fungus recorded from North America, including collections connected with bark beetles in spruce logs. It has also been isolated from logs used to grow shiitake mushrooms, where it can interfere with mushroom growth. The catalog label blue stain describes a broad type of wood discoloration, not a reliable species diagnosis. Identifying this fungus requires examination of its microscopic structures and, when needed, DNA evidence.

sources.label: Generic boundaries in the Ophiostomatales reconsidered and revised
Commodity risk assessment of maple veneer sheets from Canada, Appendix A.1.1.8

oreochromis-aureus.summary: Blue tilapia is a deep-bodied freshwater fish with a small mouth and an olive to bluish-gray back. Its tail usually has irregular markings and a pink-red outer edge; young fish show a dark spot near the rear of the dorsal fin. It occupies varied waters, from canals and vegetated lakes to rivers and springs. Females shelter eggs and young in their mouths. Introduced populations occur in Florida, where similar tilapias make careful identification important.

sources.label: Blue Tilapia Ecological Risk Screening Summary

billardiera-heterophylla.summary: Bluebell creeper is an evergreen climbing shrub from Western Australia, with slender twining stems and narrow green leaves. Small, nodding blue flowers hang in clusters and are followed by elongated purple fruits. It is grown ornamentally in mild climates and can climb through nearby vegetation. The name needs care: the similar Billardiera fusiformis is also sold and described as bluebell creeper. Older accounts under Sollya heterophylla may include both species, so identification should use a modern botanical treatment.

passiflora-caerulea.summary: Bluecrown passionflower is a vigorous climbing vine from South America. Tendrils help it grip supports, while deeply lobed leaves surround striking white flowers with a ring of blue, white and dark purple threads. Raised reproductive parts stand above the flower's center. Oval fruits ripen from green to yellow-orange. The vine remains leafy in warm winters but may lose its leaves in colder conditions. It is widely grown on fences and trellises in sunny, well-drained places.

atriplex-nummularia.summary: Bluegreen saltbush, often called old man saltbush, is a large Australian shrub with silvery-gray foliage. Tiny scales give the leaves their pale appearance; leaf shapes can vary from oval to nearly round even on one plant. Male and female flowers usually grow on separate shrubs, and the developing seeds are enclosed by enlarged, leaflike bracts. It naturally occupies inland dry country, often on heavy soils near floodways, and tolerates both drought and occasional flooding.

ageratum-houstonianum.summary: Bluemink is the familiar garden ageratum, a small annual grown for clusters of soft-looking flowers. The heads are usually blue or lavender, though cultivated forms may be pink or white. Its broad, softly hairy leaves have shallowly toothed edges, and the stems can be green or reddish. Native to Central America, it favors sunny or partly shaded, well-drained sites. It sometimes escapes cultivation, but North Carolina's flora notes that many records there represent planted specimens rather than wild populations.

sources.label: Vascular Plants of North Carolina: Floss-flower

agrilus-cyanescens.summary: The bluish borer beetle is a metallic wood-boring beetle whose adults vary from blue to green. Native to Eurasia, it is established in parts of North America. Larvae develop in woody stems of honeysuckles; a confirmed Oregon discovery involved damaged twinberry shrubs and beetles emerging from their branches. Its appearance can resemble other Agrilus beetles, so color alone is unreliable. Published assessments describe limited overall economic impact, even though individual ornamental shrubs can suffer noticeable damage.

sources.label: Westcott, Williams & Grotta (2019): Agrilus cyanescens discovered in Oregon

tradescantia-spathacea.summary: Boatlily is a tropical perennial that forms clumps of stiff, sword-shaped leaves, usually green above and purple underneath. Its small white flowers sit inside pairs of folded purple bracts that resemble little boats, explaining several of its common names. Short, thick stems keep the leaf rosettes close to the ground. Often grown as a houseplant or warm-climate groundcover, it can spread beyond gardens in suitable climates. The sap may irritate skin, so handling deserves care.

sources.label: Tradescantia spathacea: Oyster Plant, Moses in the Cradle

ficus-religiosa.summary: Bodhi tree is a large fig tree recognized by heart-shaped leaves that taper into unusually long, narrow tips. Its small figs grow near the leaf bases and turn purple to black when ripe. Native to parts of South Asia, it is widely cultivated and holds religious importance in Buddhism and Hinduism. The tree may begin life on another tree before roots reach the ground. In Singapore, birds and small mammals eat its fruits and help disperse the seeds.

sources.label: Plants of the World Online: Ficus religiosa

schoenoplectiella-mucronata.summary: Bog bulrush is a wetland sedge with upright, spongy stems that are distinctly three-sided. Its leaves are reduced largely to brown sheaths around the stem bases, so the green stems do most of the visible work. Clusters of small, cone-shaped flower spikelets produce dark brown seeds. It grows in waterlogged ground and wetlands, with a broad native range across the Old World and Australia. The names Scirpus mucronatus and Schoenoplectus mucronatus appear in older accounts of the same species.

sources.label: Plants of the World Online: Schoenoplectiella mucronata

fuchsia-boliviana.summary: Bolivian fuchsia is a large shrub or small tree from the Andes of Peru, Bolivia and northwestern Argentina. Long clusters of narrow, hanging flowers end its arching branches, usually combining scarlet tubes and petals. Broad leaves have hairy red stalks, and elongated berries darken to purple or nearly black. It is cultivated for its abundant flowers in mild, moist conditions. Some garden forms have white flower tubes with red petals, so flower color alone does not define the species.

sources.label: Plants of the World Online: Fuchsia boliviana

paraleyrodes-bondari.summary: Bondar's nesting whitefly is a tiny plant-feeding insect that leaves circular white wax deposits on foliage. Adults are about a millimeter long, with gray-brown wing bands that form an X when viewed from above. Young stages produce fine wax threads and a skirtlike fringe, eventually sitting inside a white waxy nest. Heavy infestations can coat leaves with honeydew and dark sooty mold. It has been recorded on several tropical crops and ornamentals, but related nesting whiteflies can be difficult to distinguish.

sources.label: Pest Identification Guide: Bondar's Nesting Whitefly
Distribution and Molecular Diversity of Whitefly Species Colonizing Cassava in Kenya

chrysanthemoides-monilifera.summary: Boneseed is a woody South African shrub with yellow daisy-like flowers and small fruits that turn black when ripe. The name usually refers to Chrysanthemoides monilifera subspecies monilifera, whose leathery leaves have toothed edges and whose dry seeds are pale and bone-colored. The broader species also includes bitou bush, a more spreading form with rounder, smoother-edged leaves. Introduced boneseed can form dense stands in parts of Australia and New Zealand, so the subspecies matters when describing its appearance and local behavior.

sources.label: Flora of New Zealand: Chrysanthemoides monilifera

croton-bonplandianus.summary: Bonpland's croton is a branching, partly woody plant with narrow, pointed leaves and small, inconspicuous flowers. The leaves have blunt teeth along their edges. Male and female flowers share the same flowering stem, and the rounded, three-lobed fruit separates into single-seeded sections when ripe. Native to southern South America, it has spread into many tropical regions. In India's Eastern Ghats it is naturalized in disturbed places, including clearings, village margins and fallow ground.

sources.label: Plants of the World Online: Croton bonplandianus
Digital Flora of Eastern Ghats: Croton bonplandianus
